hall.alt: Empty entrance hall with a grand staircase, carved wooden toys, warm brass lamps, and a marble compass medallion.

drawing.alt: Drawing room with a carved fireplace, burgundy sofas, a silver tea service, and tall green-draped windows.

dining.alt: Formal dining room with a long table set with china and crystal, a brass chandelier, and a carved silver-filled sideboard.

kitchen.alt: Estate kitchen with a cast-iron range, hanging copper pans, a wooden preparation table, and a checkerboard floor.

workshop.alt: Toy workshop with a workbench, an unfinished wooden automaton, carving tools, clockwork toys, and a mechanical orrery.

library.alt: Library with towering bookshelves, a rolling ladder, green leather armchairs, an open atlas, and an antique globe.

study.alt: William’s private study with a green-leather writing desk, toy designs, a closed wall safe, and a fireside seating area.

billiards.alt: Billiard room with a green table, brass-shaded lamps, a cue rack, leather chairs, and dark walnut paneling.

music.alt: Music room with a grand piano, a violin, a brass-horn phonograph, and upholstered listening chairs.

conservatory.alt: Glass-roofed conservatory with lush palms and orchids, a central fountain, wicker seating, and warm hanging lanterns.

study.title: The study is sealed
study.speaker: Officer Frank Donnelly
study.text: I’m sorry, but the study is off limits for now. We’re still collecting evidence and arranging for Mr. Thoreson’s body to be taken to the morgue. Please leave everything undisturbed. I’ll let you know when you may enter.

steps.label: Act 2 · A death at the estate
steps.text: Ladies and gentlemen, may I have your attention. I’m Officer Frank Donnelly, Dallas Police. I’m afraid I have some very difficult news.
steps.phoneText: Ladies and gentlemen, may I have your attention. I’m Officer Frank Donnelly, Dallas Police. I’m afraid I have some very difficult news.

steps.label: Act 2 · A death at the estate
steps.text: William Thoreson has been found dead in his study.
steps.phoneText: William Thoreson has been found dead in his study.

steps.label: Act 2 · A death at the estate
steps.text: I cannot yet tell you precisely what happened. But I have seen enough to believe his death was no accident. Until we know otherwise, I am treating this as a murder.
steps.phoneText: I cannot yet tell you precisely what happened. But I have seen enough to believe his death was no accident. Until we know otherwise, I am treating this as a murder.

steps.label: Act 2 · A death at the estate
steps.text: The storm has made the roads nearly impassable. I’ve requested a detective and transport from the morgue, but neither will reach us soon. For the moment, you have me.

steps.label: Act 2 · A death at the estate
steps.text: Some of you knew his business. Some knew his family. Some, I suspect, knew things he preferred to keep private.

reward.name: Confession Recording — Transcript
reward.text:
I need to confess something. Before it's too late. I don't know how much time I have left. So I'm recording this. For my family. For the truth. Robert Hartley was my partner. He was my closest friend. We built that company together. Thoreson & Hartley Toys. And I betrayed him.

[static]

I am not a good man. Robert found out.

[static]

He was furious. Rightfully so. He came to me and said he would pull every dollar he had out of the company. That he'd burn it to the ground before he'd let me profit from it. He said I'd taken everything from him. And he was right. So I acted first. I forged his signature on a transfer document. I took the company. Everything Robert had built — I put it in my name before he could destroy it. I told myself I was protecting the business. That was a lie. I was protecting myself. Robert died the next day. I took his company.

[static]

It broke him. They ruled it a suicide. But I know what really killed Robert Hartley. It was me.

[static]

After Robert died,

[static]

I didn't want anyone to know what I'd done.

[static]

That was my doing. I've carried this guilt for twenty-five years. But tonight,

[static]

Though God knows I don't deserve it.

[static]

It's time to tell the truth. I only pray it isn't too late.

interactions.name: Harmonic Listening Cabinet
interactions.description: William’s unmistakable craftsmanship is everywhere: a polished wooden cabinet, exposed clockwork gears and a tiny toy conductor poised with his baton raised. An absurdly large brass ear sprouts from one side, aimed at the piano. The hand-engraved plaque reads: W. THORESON — AUTOMATIC MUSICAL APPRECIATOR. Only William would have built such a strange contraption.
interactions.lockedText: Locked. The little conductor will not budge. Beneath the brass ear, a needle quivers at nearby sounds. It almost seems to be listening—perhaps waiting for a particular tune.

interactions.name: A letter from William
interactions.description: A folded sheet of cream stationery, covered in William’s sprawling handwriting. The heading reads: “On the Importance of Aiming High.”

reward.name: On the Importance of Aiming High
reward.text:
My dear friends,

We should all reach for the stars—in our work, our fortunes, and our health. Though I recommend keeping both feet on the floor when attempting it before breakfast.

The same ambition applies to that peculiar pastime involving a stick, a few balls, and gentlemen who insist that missing was part of the plan. A little direction can do wonders. So can knowing when to take your cue.

Do not let anyone clip your wings. If my little bird is in your keeping, perhaps it is your turn to take a shot. Let its name guide your aim, one letter at a time.

After all, even the grandest flight begins with a small leap of faith—and occasionally ends in a pocket.

Yours, with lofty intentions,
William

interactions.name: Officer Donnelly
interactions.description: Officer Donnelly stands near the entrance, keeping watch beside a board of collected evidence.

reward.name: A word with Donnelly
reward.text: “If you need a direction, ask. Otherwise, I shall leave you to form your own conclusions.”

guidance.text: “People leave the oddest things among the everyday clutter. Have you looked inside the kitchen drawers?”
“There was a folded letter in that kitchen drawer. It may be worth bringing along rather than leaving it where you found it.”
“William’s letter talks a good deal about taking a shot. Perhaps compare it with what you find by the billiards table—and with the belongings he left you.”
“I heard something click beneath the billiards table. An open drawer is worth a closer inspection.”
“You have made a start. Try examining the piano in the music room. William seems to have left more than entertainment behind.”
“Look through the music you have found, and talk about what each of you knows of William. There may be a reason he kept those particular sheets.”
“That strange cabinet by the piano has stirred. See what it was keeping safe.”
“Not everything in a workshop is a puzzle. A plain storage cabinet can be worth opening too.”
“You noticed something on the workshop cabinet shelf. Have you taken a closer look at it?”
“You have gathered a few useful things. Try them on the mechanisms you have not yet managed to operate.”
“Bring your evidence to the board beside me. Compare what the documents actually say with what people have told you. I shall not make your conclusions for you.”
